content:
Claude Code's auto mode will become the default permission setting for users next week.

Starting August 14, conversations for Pro, Max, and Team users will use auto mode unless users or administrators have locked in different settings.

Anthropic will no longer charge for the additional tokens generated by the auto mode classifier on each tool call.

According to Anthropic, auto mode uses a classifier to replace recurring authorization prompts, checking whether each tool call involves irreversible, destructive, or out-of-scope actions.

If the classifier blocks an action, Claude can attempt a safer approach or request authorization from the user. After multiple blocks, the conversation will revert to manual authorization mode.

As part of this adjustment, Anthropic said it will no longer charge for the "small amount of additional tokens generated per tool call" by the auto mode classifier.

Anthropic stated that they studied 1,053 paid testers and found that humans only blocked 13.6% of dangerous commands, while auto mode blocked 89%. After 50 prompts, human performance dropped to about 5%.

However, Anthropic also pointed out that the classifier cannot completely eliminate risk, and recommended that production environment changes should still be reviewed manually.

This adjustment is expected to make executing long-duration tasks through Claude Code more practically viable, and will work in conjunction with its general workflow, voice mode, and the browser built into the Mac application. Anthropic stated that Team and Enterprise customers using auto mode submitted approximately 25% more pull requests.

9to5Mac's Take

Although it sounds somewhat risky, for experienced users, this may be a reasonable default setting. However, users should establish a certain level of trust with the coding agent before relying on auto mode.

It is worth noting the approach Anthropic has taken. For comparison, OpenAI previously turned off auto mode for its most powerful GPT-5.6 version out of additional caution.
